qs.q: Why can a very large array fail to be allocated even when the total amount of free memory is sufficient?

c.x: Free memory may be fragmented, and an array needs one contiguous block
Arrays must store a pointer to the next element, which doubles their size
Arrays can only be allocated when their size is a power of two
Arrays are stored in non-contiguous blocks, which are scarce in memory

qs.e: An array requires contiguous memory. If the free memory is split into small separate pieces, no single piece may be large enough, even though the total free space is enough. Linked lists avoid this problem because their nodes can be stored anywhere in memory.

qs.q: In a singly linked list, why is accessing the element at position $k$ an $O(n)$ operation, unlike in an array where it is $O(1)$?

c.x: Each node stores its own index, which must be recomputed on every access
The list must first be copied into contiguous memory before indexing
Nodes can only be reached by following next references from the head one by one
The nodes are stored in sorted order and need a binary search to be found

e: An array stores elements contiguously, so the address of element $k$ is computed directly (random access) in $O(1)$.
A linked list stores nodes in non-contiguous locations, so there is no formula that gives the address of node $k$.
The only way to reach node $k$ is to start at the head and follow the next reference $k$ times.
<mark>This sequential access costs $O(n)$ in the worst case.</mark>

qs.q: Which pair of components makes up a single node of a singly linked list?

c.x: An index and the value of the element
The element's data and a reference to the next node
The element's data and a reference to the previous node
A reference to the head and a reference to the tail

qs.e: Each node of a singly linked list holds the data (the element) and a reference that stores the address of the next node. A reference to the previous node exists only in doubly linked lists.

qs.q: While traversing a singly linked list from its head, how can the tail be identified?

c.x: It is the node whose data field is `None`
It is the node that the head references directly
It is the node whose next reference points back to the head
It is the node whose next reference is `None`

qs.e: Starting at the head and following each next reference eventually reaches a node whose next reference is `None`. That node is the tail. (Pointing back to the head is the property of a circularly linked list.)

qs.q: A singly linked list keeps only a head reference. What is the main benefit of also storing an explicit tail reference?

c.x: Elements can be accessed by index in $O(1)$ time
Nodes no longer need to store a next reference
The last node is reached directly, without traversing the list
Insertion at the head becomes faster than before

e: With only a head reference, reaching the last node requires following $n-1$ next references.
An explicit tail reference gives direct access to the last node, so operations such as add_last do not need to traverse the list.
Insertion at the head was already $O(1)$, and the nodes still need their next references.
<mark>The tail reference avoids traversing the list to find the last node.</mark>

qs.q: In add_first, the lecture runs `newest.next = L.head` first and only then `L.head = newest`. What happens if these two statements are swapped?

c.x: The new node's next references itself, so the old nodes are lost
The new node is inserted at the tail instead of the head
The list works normally, because the order does not matter
The size counter becomes wrong, but all links stay correct

e: After the swap, `L.head = newest` runs first, so the head now references the new node.
Then `newest.next = L.head` reads the head, which is now `newest` itself.
So the new node's next references itself, and the old first node is no longer reachable from the head.
<mark>The order matters: first link the new node to the old head, then move the head.</mark>

qs.q: A singly linked list (with head, tail and size) holds `MSP -> ATL -> BOS` with `size = 3`. The operations `add_first(L, 'LAX')` and then `add_last(L, 'MIA')` are performed. What are the final order of nodes and the size?

c.x: `MIA -> LAX -> MSP -> ATL -> BOS`, size 5
`LAX -> MSP -> ATL -> BOS -> MIA`, size 5
`LAX -> MSP -> ATL -> BOS -> MIA`, size 4
`MSP -> ATL -> BOS -> LAX -> MIA`, size 5

e: Initial list: `MSP -> ATL -> BOS`, `size = 3`.
`add_first(L, 'LAX')`: the new node points to the old head `MSP` and becomes the head, so the list is `LAX -> MSP -> ATL -> BOS` and `size = 4`.
`add_last(L, 'MIA')`: the old tail `BOS` points to the new node, which becomes the tail, so the list is `LAX -> MSP -> ATL -> BOS -> MIA` and `size = 5`.
<mark>Final list: `LAX -> MSP -> ATL -> BOS -> MIA`, with size 5.</mark>

qs.q: Why does LinkedStack place the top of the stack at the <u>head</u> of the list rather than at the tail?

c.x: Nodes at the tail of a list cannot store data elements
A singly linked list cannot be modified at its tail at all
The head node is always allocated before all other nodes
Constant-time insertion and deletion are possible only at the head

e: Insertion at the head is $O(1)$: create a node and make it point to the old head.
Deletion at the head is $O(1)$: move the head to the next node.
Deleting the tail would require finding the node before it, and a singly linked list cannot move backwards, so a traversal of $O(n)$ would be needed.
<mark>So the top of the stack is kept at the head, where push and pop take constant time.</mark>

qs.q: Why can a linked list grow without declaring its size in advance?

c.x: It reserves a large contiguous block and doubles it when full
It shifts all existing elements to make room for a new one
Nodes are allocated one at a time and linked as elements are added
Each node reserves space for all the elements that may come later

qs.e: A linked list allocates memory one node at a time, only when an element is added, and connects the new node using references. Therefore its size is dynamic and no space is wasted in advance.

qs.q:
Consider the following code:
```python
s = LinkedStack()
s.push(5)
s.push(8)
s.push(3)
s.pop()
```
What does `s.top()` return now, and what is `len(s)`?
e: `push(5)`: the stack is `5` (top), size 1.
`push(8)`: the new node becomes the head, so the stack is `8, 5` (top first), size 2.
`push(3)`: the stack is `3, 8, 5`, size 3.
`pop()`: removes and returns the top element `3`; the head moves to the node holding `8`, and size becomes 2.
<mark>`s.top()` returns `8` and `len(s)` is `2`.</mark>

qs.q: How do the time bounds of LinkedStack operations compare with those of ArrayStack?

c.x: LinkedStack operations are amortized $O(1)$, while ArrayStack gives worst-case $O(1)$
Both structures take $O(n)$ in the worst case for every `push`
LinkedStack operations are worst-case $O(1)$, while ArrayStack gives amortized $O(1)$
LinkedStack `pop` takes $O(n)$ because it must traverse to the tail

e: Every LinkedStack method (`push`, `pop`, `top`, `len`, `is_empty`) does a fixed number of steps, so each runs in worst-case $O(1)$.
ArrayStack occasionally has to resize its underlying array, which costs $O(n)$ for that single operation, so its bound is only amortized $O(1)$.
<mark>LinkedStack: worst-case constant time; ArrayStack: amortized constant time.</mark>

qs.q: What does the single statement `self._head = self._Node(e, self._head)` do inside `push`?

c.x: It creates a node whose next is the old head, then makes it the new head
It creates a node at the tail and links the old head after it
It replaces the data stored in the current head node with `e`
It creates a node whose next is `None` and discards the old head

e: The right side `self._Node(e, self._head)` creates a node storing `e` whose next reference is the old head.
The assignment then makes `self._head` reference this new node.
<mark>The new node is linked in front of the old nodes, which is exactly what a push at the top of the stack needs.</mark>

qs.q: Why does LinkedQueue maintain <u>both</u> `_head` and `_tail` references, while LinkedStack needs only `_head`?

c.x: Queue nodes need two references to store their elements
A queue must be traversed from tail to head on every operation
A stack cannot keep a reference to a tail node
Queue operations work on both ends: enqueue at the tail, dequeue at the head

e: A stack inserts and removes at the same end (the head), so a head reference is enough.
A queue is FIFO: dequeue removes from the head and enqueue adds at the tail.
Without a tail reference, every enqueue would have to traverse the list to find the last node.
<mark>Keeping both references makes both queue operations $O(1)$.</mark>

qs.q: A new `LinkedQueue` is empty. After `enqueue(7)`, which description of its state is correct?

c.x: `_head` references the new node, but `_tail` remains `None`
`_head` and `_tail` both reference the new node, and `_size` is 1
`_tail` references the new node, but `_head` remains `None`
`_head` and `_tail` both stay `None` until a second element arrives

e: `enqueue` creates `newest = self._Node(7, None)`.
Since the queue is empty, the special case runs: `self._head = newest`.
Then `self._tail = newest` runs (for every enqueue) and `self._size` becomes 1.
<mark>The single node is both the head and the tail.</mark>

qs.q: Starting from an empty `LinkedQueue`, these operations are executed: `enqueue('A')`, `enqueue('B')`, `enqueue('C')`, `dequeue()`, `dequeue()`. What is the final state?

c.x: Front is `'B'`, size is 2, and `_head` and `_tail` reference the same node
Front is `'B'`, size is 1, and `_tail` is `None`
Front is `'C'`, size is 1, and `_head` and `_tail` reference the same node
Front is `'C'`, size is 2, and `_head` is `None`

e: After the three enqueues the queue is `A, B, C` (front to back), size 3.
First `dequeue()`: returns `'A'`, the head moves to `B`, size 2.
Second `dequeue()`: returns `'B'`, the head moves to `C`, size 1. The queue is not empty, so `_tail` is not reset.
Now only `C` remains, and it is both the head and the tail.
<mark>Front is `'C'`, size is 1, and `_head` and `_tail` reference the same node.</mark>

qs.q: In `LinkedQueue.dequeue`, the code sets `self._tail = None` when the queue becomes empty. Why is this special case needed?

c.x: Setting `_tail` to `None` is what decrements `_size`
Without it, `_head` would keep referencing the removed node
Without it, the next `enqueue` would raise an `Empty` exception
The removed head was also the tail, so `_tail` would still reference a removed node

e: `dequeue` only updates the head: `self._head = self._head._next`.
If the queue had a single node, that node was both the head and the tail, and the new head becomes `None`.
The tail is not touched by that statement, so it would still reference the node that was just removed.
<mark>Setting `_tail = None` keeps the state consistent: an empty queue has both `_head` and `_tail` equal to `None`.</mark>

qs.q: What distinguishes a circularly linked list from an ordinary singly linked list?

c.x: The tail's next reference points back to the head, not to `None`
Every node stores both a next and a previous reference
The head's next reference is `None`, which marks the list start
The list can only hold a fixed number of nodes

qs.e: In a circularly linked list the tail uses its next reference to point back to the head, so the list forms a circle and no node has `None` as its next reference. <mark>Following next references never ends unless you stop on purpose.</mark>

qs.q: A `CircularQueue` stores only `_tail` and `_size`. How does it reach the front of the queue in constant time?

c.x: By reading `self._head`, which is updated on every enqueue
By reading `self._tail._next`, since the tail points back to the head
By traversing from the tail until a `None` reference is found
By reading `self._tail._previous`, the node just before the tail

e: In a circular list the tail's next reference points to the head.
So the front of the queue is `self._tail._next`, reached in one step.
<mark>One reference (`_tail`) gives access to both ends: the tail directly and the head through `_tail._next`.</mark>

qs.q: In round-robin scheduling, the steps are: dequeue the next element, service it, then enqueue it again. Which action in `CircularQueue` achieves the dequeue-and-re-enqueue effect without creating or removing any node?

c.x: Calling `dequeue()` and then `enqueue()` with the returned element
Calling `first()` twice and then `dequeue()` once
Calling `rotate()`, which only moves the `_tail` reference
Calling `enqueue()` first and then `dequeue()` once

e: `rotate()` runs `self._tail = self._tail._next`.
The old head becomes the new tail, so the front element moves to the back of the queue.
No node is created or deleted; only one reference changes, so it takes $O(1)$.
<mark>`rotate()` is the efficient way to give each process its turn in round-robin order.</mark>

qs.q: A `CircularQueue` holds `A, B, C, D` from front to back. After one call to `rotate()`, what are the front and the tail?

c.x: Front `A`, tail `D`
Front `D`, tail `C`
Front `C`, tail `B`
Front `B`, tail `A`

e: Before: tail is `D`, so the front is `D._next = A`.
`rotate()` sets `_tail = _tail._next`, so the tail becomes `A`.
The new front is `A._next = B`, so the order becomes `B, C, D, A`.
<mark>Front is `B` and tail is `A`.</mark>

qs.q: A `CircularQueue` holds `P1, P2, P3` from front to back. After 5 consecutive calls to `rotate()`, which process is at the front?

c.x: No process, because the queue becomes empty

e: Each `rotate()` moves the front element to the back, so the order cycles every 3 calls.
After 1 rotate: `P2, P3, P1`. After 2: `P3, P1, P2`. After 3: `P1, P2, P3`.
After 4: `P2, P3, P1`. After 5: `P3, P1, P2`.
Shortcut: the front after $k$ rotations is the element at index $k \bmod 3$, and $5 \bmod 3 = 2$, which is `P3` (index 2, counting from 0).
<mark>The front is `P3`.</mark>

qs.q: In `CircularQueue.enqueue` on a non-empty queue, the code runs `newest._next = self._tail._next` <u>before</u> `self._tail._next = newest`. What goes wrong if the two lines are swapped?

c.x: The new node becomes the head instead of the tail
The new node references itself, so the old head becomes unreachable
The size counter is incremented twice
The old tail's next reference becomes `None`

e: After the swap, `self._tail._next = newest` runs first, so the old tail now points to the new node.
Then `newest._next = self._tail._next` reads `self._tail._next`, which is now `newest` itself.
So the new node points to itself, and nothing references the old head any more (the head was only reachable through the tail's next).
<mark>The new node must first copy the old head reference, and only then be linked after the old tail.</mark>

qs.q: When `enqueue` is called on an <u>empty</u> `CircularQueue`, why does the code set `newest._next = newest`?

c.x: To mark the queue as empty using a self-reference
To make the new node reference the old tail
To store the element twice for extra safety
A one-node circular list must have its next point back to itself

e: In a circular list the tail's next reference must point to the head.
When there is only one node, it is both the head and the tail.
<mark>So its next reference must point back to itself, and the node then becomes `_tail`.</mark>

qs.q: A `CircularQueue` holds `A, B, C` from front to back, so `_tail` references `C`. After `dequeue()`, what is returned and what does `_tail._next` reference?

c.x: Returns `A`; `_tail._next` references `A`
Returns `A`; `_tail._next` references `B`
Returns `C`; `_tail._next` references `B`
Returns `B`; `_tail._next` references `C`

e: `oldhead = self._tail._next`, which is `A`.
The size is 3 (not 1), so the else branch runs: `self._tail._next = oldhead._next`, which is `B`.
The size becomes 2 and the method returns `oldhead._element`, which is `A`.
<mark>Returns `A`, and the tail now points to `B` as the new head.</mark>

qs.q: Which operation is generally more efficient on a linked list than on an array?

c.x: Reading the $i$-th element directly by index
Inserting a new element at the front without shifting elements
Storing all elements in a single contiguous block
Using less memory for each stored element

qs.e: Inserting at the front of an array requires shifting all elements, which is costly. In a linked list only a few references change, so it is $O(1)$. <mark>Index access is better in arrays, and linked lists use extra memory for references.</mark>

qs.q: A program receives an unpredictable number of items, inserts most of them at the front, and rarely reads an item by position. Which structure fits best?

c.x: A fixed-size array, allocated for the largest expected number of items
An ordered array, kept sorted after every insertion
A singly linked list, which inserts at the head in constant time
An array that is completely re-created after each insertion

e: The number of items is unknown, so a dynamic size is needed; arrays are fixed in size or must be re-allocated.
Frequent insertion at the front would force an array to shift all elements each time, costing $O(n)$.
Index access is rare, so the $O(n)$ sequential access of a linked list is not a problem.
<mark>A singly linked list fits best: dynamic size and $O(1)$ insertion at the head.</mark>

qs.q: Why does `remove_first(L)` first check whether `L.head` is `None`?

c.x: To reset the size counter to zero before removing
To avoid accessing `L.head.next` when the list is empty
To find the tail before the head is removed
To confirm that the list is sorted before removal

qs.e: If the list is empty, `L.head` is `None`, so evaluating `L.head.next` would fail. <mark>The algorithm therefore reports an error for an empty list before trying to remove anything.</mark>

qs.q: A singly linked list has $n$ nodes and a reference only to the head. How many `next` hops are needed to reach the last node, and what does this imply?

c.x: $1$ hop, so reaching the tail is $O(1)$
$n$ hops, so reaching the tail is $O(\log n)$
$n+1$ hops, so reaching the tail is $O(n^2)$
$n-1$ hops, so reaching the tail is $O(n)$

e: The head is node 1 and the tail is node $n$.
Each hop moves forward by one node, so going from node 1 to node $n$ takes $n-1$ hops.
The number of hops grows linearly with $n$.
<mark>$n-1$ hops, so reaching the tail is $O(n)$, which is why storing an explicit tail reference is useful.</mark>

qs.q: The head references address `1000`. Memory holds these nodes: address `1000` stores (data `5`, next `2400`); address `2400` stores (data `9`, next `1800`); address `1800` stores (data `2`, next `NULL`). In what order does a traversal visit the data?
e: Start at the head, address `1000`: visit data `5`; its next is `2400`.
Go to address `2400`: visit data `9`; its next is `1800`.
Go to address `1800`: visit data `2`; its next is `NULL`, so this is the tail and the traversal stops.
<mark>The traversal order is `5, 9, 2`, which follows the links and not the memory addresses.</mark>

qs.q: In add_last, suppose `L.tail = newest` runs before `L.tail.next = newest`. What is the result?

c.x: The new node is appended correctly and only `size` is wrong
The new node is inserted at the head instead of the tail
The old tail is never linked to the new node, which points to itself
The old tail is removed from the list

e: After the swap, `L.tail = newest` runs first, so the tail variable now references the new node.
Then `L.tail.next = newest` sets the next of the new node (the current tail) to itself.
The old tail's next is never updated, so the new node is not reachable from the head, and it points to itself.
<mark>The old tail must be linked to the new node first, and only then should the tail variable be updated.</mark>
